\chapter{Four Adjectives That Always Agree}
\label{ch:hi-adjectives-that-bend}
\hlchaptermodality{90}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can describe a person as tall, short, thin or stout, and make each adjective agree, because all four end in -aa.}

Say the same sentence about a man and about a woman, and hear that vah and hai never move while the adjective carries the whole gender load.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[lambā]{\hi{लंबा} — tall and long are the same word, and this one bends}

\label{lesson:HI-C82-lambaa}



\begin{quote}
The last chapter gave you four adjectives and \textbf{not one of them changed its ending}. Say \textbf{\hi{आसान}} and remember why it stayed put. This chapter gives you three that do the opposite, and you can see it coming from the spelling.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \hi{लंबा}}
\textbf{\hi{लंबा}} (\emph{lambā}) — \textquotedblleft{}tall,\textquotedblright{} and also \textquotedblleft{}long.\textquotedblright{}

Hindi does not split those two. A person is \emph{lambā}, a road is \emph{lambā}, a film is \emph{lambā}. English keeps three words for one measurement and chooses between them by what the thing is doing: \textbf{tall} if it stands up, \textbf{long} if it lies down, \textbf{lengthy} if it is made of time. Hindi measures the distance and stops there.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\hi{लंबा}} is Sanskrit \textbf{\hi{लम्ब}} (\emph{lamba}), \textquotedblleft{}hanging down, drooping.\textquotedblright{} The idea began as \emph{what dangles} — and a thing that dangles is measured by how far down it reaches.

That root travelled. Latin \textbf{limbus} is a hanging border or hem, and English took it twice:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{word} & \textbf{the hanging thing} \\
\midrule
\textbf{limb} & what hangs off the trunk \\
\textbf{limbo} & the \emph{edge}, the hem of things \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

So \textbf{\hi{लंबा}} and English \textbf{limb} are the same old idea about hanging, arrived at from opposite ends of a continent.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: this one ends in -\hi{आ}, so it bends}]
Nothing new here — the shape you already learned, meeting a new word:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{shape} & \textbf{masculine singular} & \textbf{feminine} \\
\midrule
ends in \textbf{-\hi{आ}} & \hi{लंबा} & \hi{लंबी} \\
ends in a consonant & \hi{आसान} & \hi{आसान} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\textbf{\hi{लंबा}} ends in \textbf{-\hi{आ}}, so it behaves like \textbf{\hi{काला}}: \emph{lambā} for a man, \emph{lambī} for a woman, \emph{lambe} for more than one man.

This is the whole reason the easy-and-difficult lesson and this one belong next to each other. That one gave you four adjectives that never move, and every one of them ended in a consonant. These three all end in \textbf{-\hi{आ}}, and every one of them moves. Nothing has to be memorised — look at the last letter.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}\hi{लंबा}\textquotedblright{} — \emph{lambā}, tall
  \item the form you would use about a woman (\emph{lambī})
  \item \textquotedblleft{}\hi{लंबा} \hi{रास्ता}\textquotedblright{} — a long road, the same word doing the other job
  \item which English word for an arm or a leg comes from the same root (\emph{limb})
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How many English words does \textbf{\hi{लंबा}} cover? (At least three: tall, long, lengthy.) What did the Sanskrit root mean? (Hanging down.) What tells you this adjective will bend? (It ends in \textbf{-\hi{आ}}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[patlā]{\hi{पतला} — thin, and a root that fell over}

\label{lesson:HI-C82-patlaa}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{\hi{लंबा}} and its feminine form. The next word has the same ending, so you already know what it will do.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \hi{पतला}}
\textbf{\hi{पतला}} (\emph{patlā}) — \textquotedblleft{}thin.\textquotedblright{}

It works for a person, for a sheet of paper, and for a soup that has too much water in it. English needs \emph{thin}, \emph{slim}, \emph{slender} and \emph{watery} for that range; Hindi uses one word and lets the noun decide which English word you would have reached for.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\hi{पतला}} goes back to Sanskrit \textbf{\hi{पत्र}} and the root \textbf{\hi{पत्}} (\emph{pat}), \textquotedblleft{}to fall.\textquotedblright{} A thin thing is one that has \textbf{fallen flat} — flattened out until there is hardly anything left of it.

The same root is sitting in two Hindi words you may already recognise:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{word} & \textbf{the falling in it} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\hi{पत्ता}} (\emph{pattā}) & a leaf — the thing that falls \\
\emph{patjhaṛ} & autumn — literally the leaf-fall \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Autumn in Hindi is named exactly the way American English names it: \textbf{fall}. Two languages that never discussed it reached for the same picture.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the second of the three}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{adjective} & \textbf{masculine} & \textbf{feminine} \\
\midrule
\hi{लंबा} & \hi{लंबा} & \hi{लंबी} \\
\hi{पतला} & \hi{पतला} & \hi{पतली} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Same ending, same behaviour, no exception to learn. This is what a rule that actually works looks like: you were told the shape, and every new word that has the shape does the thing.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}\hi{पतला}\textquotedblright{} — \emph{patlā}, thin
  \item the feminine form (\emph{patlī})
  \item \emph{lambā aur patlā} — tall and thin, both bending the same way
  \item what Hindi calls autumn, and what it literally means (\emph{patjhaṛ}, the leaf-fall)
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What did the Sanskrit root \textbf{\hi{पत्}} mean? (To fall.) What is a thin thing, by that picture? (Something flattened, fallen out flat.) Which English name for autumn matches the Hindi one? (\emph{Fall}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[moṭā]{\hi{मोटा} — thick, and the word that refuses to be only about people}

\label{lesson:HI-C82-motaa}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{\hi{पतला}} and its feminine. The word in this lesson is its opposite, and it ends the same way.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \hi{मोटा}}
\textbf{\hi{मोटा}} (\emph{moṭā}) — \textquotedblleft{}thick, stout, heavy.\textquotedblright{}

Set it against \textbf{\hi{पतला}} and the pair covers the whole range at once:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{thing} & \textbf{\hi{पतला}} & \textbf{\hi{मोटा}} \\
\midrule
a person & slim & stout \\
a rope & thin & thick \\
a book & slim & fat \\
a voice & reedy & deep \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

That last row is the one to keep. A \textbf{\hi{मोटी} \hi{आवाज़}} is a \emph{deep} voice, not a fat one — the metaphor runs from the thickness of the string to the lowness of the note, exactly as it does on any instrument.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\hi{मोटा}} is from Sanskrit \textbf{\hi{मूर्त}} by way of Prakrit, carrying the sense of something \textbf{solid, with body to it} — a shape that has taken form rather than staying an outline.

Hindi extends it to mean \textbf{rough or approximate}, which follows from the same picture: a \emph{\hi{मोटा}} estimate is one drawn with a thick line rather than a thin one, so it has no fine detail. English does this with \textbf{broadly}, and the metaphor is identical.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: all three of them, and the rule holds}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{adjective} & \textbf{masculine} & \textbf{feminine} \\
\midrule
\hi{लंबा} & \hi{लंबा} & \hi{लंबी} \\
\hi{पतला} & \hi{पतला} & \hi{पतली} \\
\hi{मोटा} & \hi{मोटा} & \hi{मोटी} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Three words, one ending, one behaviour. Against the four from the last chapter — none of which ended in \textbf{-\hi{आ}} and none of which moved — that is the cleanest demonstration this book can give you that the ending is the rule.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}\hi{मोटा}\textquotedblright{} — \emph{moṭā}, thick
  \item the feminine form (\emph{moṭī})
  \item \emph{patlā aur moṭā} — the pair
  \item what a \textbf{\hi{मोटी} \hi{आवाज़}} is (a deep voice)
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \textbf{\hi{मोटा}} mean when it describes a voice? (Deep.) And when it describes an estimate? (Rough, approximate.) Does it bend? (Yes — it ends in \textbf{-\hi{आ}}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[nāṭā]{\hi{नाटा} — the gap that a word you already knew could not fill}

\label{lesson:HI-C82-naataa}



\begin{quote}
You have \textbf{\hi{लंबा}} for tall. Reach for its opposite using a word you already know, and then read on to find out why that reach does not work.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \hi{नाटा}}
\textbf{\hi{नाटा}} (\emph{nāṭā}) — \textquotedblleft{}short, of a person's height.\textquotedblright{}

The obvious guess is \emph{choṭā}, and the obvious guess is wrong — not because it is rude, but because it means something else.

\begin{cousinweb}
This is the clearest case in the chapter of a word existing because another word is busy:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{word} & \textbf{about a thing} & \textbf{about a person} \\
\midrule
\emph{choṭā} & small & \textbf{younger} \\
\textbf{\hi{नाटा}} & — & \textbf{short in height} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\emph{Choṭā bhāī} is a younger brother regardless of how tall he is. Hindi took the size word for a person's age and left the height meaning without an owner, and \textbf{\hi{नाटा}} is what filled the hole.

Sanskrit \textbf{\hi{नत}} (\emph{nata}) is behind it, meaning \textbf{bent, bowed, stooping} — the same root as \emph{namaste}, where the bowing is a greeting. A \emph{nāṭā} person is pictured as one closer to the ground.

A note on using it. \textbf{\hi{नाटा}} is plain rather than polite, and about a person it can land as blunt. When you want neutral, Hindi says \emph{qad meṅ choṭā}, \textquotedblleft{}short in height\textquotedblright{} — which spells out the \emph{height} part that \emph{choṭā} on its own leaves ambiguous. Recognise \textbf{\hi{नाटा}}; reach for the longer phrase.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the fourth of four, and the rule has not moved}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{adjective} & \textbf{masculine} & \textbf{feminine} \\
\midrule
\hi{लंबा} & \hi{लंबा} & \hi{लंबी} \\
\hi{पतला} & \hi{पतला} & \hi{पतली} \\
\hi{मोटा} & \hi{मोटा} & \hi{मोटी} \\
\hi{नाटा} & \hi{नाटा} & \hi{नाटी} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Four words for the shape of a person, all four ending in \textbf{-\hi{आ}}, all four bending. You can now answer a question about anyone's build without once needing to remember which words agree.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}\hi{नाटा}\textquotedblright{} — \emph{nāṭā}, short
  \item the feminine form (\emph{nāṭī})
  \item \emph{lambā} and its real opposite, rather than the one you first reached for
  \item the neutral phrase for short in height (\emph{qad meṅ choṭā})
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Why can \emph{choṭā} not mean \emph{short} about a person? (About a person it means \emph{younger}.) What did the Sanskrit root behind \textbf{\hi{नाटा}} mean? (Bent or bowed — the same idea as the bow in \emph{namaste}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[baṛā, choṭā, lambā, nāṭā, patlā, moṭā]{chhah ākār — six shapes, and the two that were only ever about things}

\label{lesson:HI-C82-repaso-shareer}



\begin{quote}
Name the four new adjectives with their feminine forms before reading on.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: which ones a person can be}]
You had two size words already, and they were taught about objects. The four new ones are the ones a person gets described with:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{adjective} & \textbf{feminine} & \textbf{used of a person?} \\
\midrule
\hi{बड़ा} & \hi{बड़ी} & as \emph{elder}, not as \emph{large} \\
\emph{choṭā} & \emph{choṭī} & as \emph{younger}, not as \emph{small} \\
\hi{लंबा} & \hi{लंबी} & yes — tall \\
\hi{नाटा} & \hi{नाटी} & yes — short in height \\
\hi{पतला} & \hi{पतली} & yes — thin \\
\hi{मोटा} & \hi{मोटी} & yes — stout \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

The first two rows are the ones worth pausing on. \textbf{\hi{बड़ा}} and \emph{choṭā} applied to a person almost always mean \textbf{older} and \textbf{younger}, not big and small — \emph{baṛā bhāī} is an elder brother, whatever his height. So the track could size a box long before it could describe a body, which is why these four were needed — and why \emph{nāṭā} had to be a separate word rather than a reuse of \emph{choṭā}.

All six end in \textbf{-\hi{आ}}. All six bend. That is not a coincidence: size and shape words are old inherited vocabulary, and inherited Hindi adjectives are the ones that kept the ending.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item all six in the masculine, then all six in the feminine
  \item which two mean \emph{older} and \emph{younger} when they describe a person
  \item \emph{lambā aur patlā}, then the same about a woman
  \item the one that also means \emph{deep}, about a voice (\emph{moṭā})
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \textbf{\hi{बड़ा} \hi{भाई}} mean — a big brother or an elder one? (An elder one.) Which of the six bend? (All of them: every one ends in \textbf{-\hi{आ}}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[vah lambī hai]{\hi{वह} \hi{लंबी} \hi{है} — the sentence that makes you choose the ending}

\label{lesson:HI-C82-sintesis-shareer}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{\hi{लंबा}} and \textbf{\hi{पतला}}. In a list they sit still. In a sentence about a real person they will not.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the ending is chosen by who you are talking about}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{about} & \textbf{sentence} & \textbf{the ending} \\
\midrule
a man & \hi{वह} \hi{लंबा} \hi{है} & \textbf{-\hi{आ}} \\
a woman & \hi{वह} \hi{लंबी} \hi{है} & \textbf{-\hi{ई}} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\textbf{\hi{वह}} does not change. \textbf{\hi{है}} does not change. The adjective carries the whole load, which is the opposite of English, where \emph{he} and \emph{she} do the work and \emph{tall} never moves.

That is worth saying plainly: in English the pronoun tells you the gender and the adjective is inert. In Hindi the pronoun is silent about it and the adjective tells you. A listener who misses the ending has missed the information.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,skin=enhanced,colback=orange!6,colframe=orange!45!black,boxrule=0.5pt,arc=1mm,left=6pt,right=6pt,top=4pt,bottom=4pt,fonttitle=\bfseries,title={Read this}]
Read aloud. Every word has been taught:

\begin{quote}
\hi{वह} \hi{लंबी} \hi{है।} \hi{वह} \hi{पतली} \hi{है।} \hi{वह} \hi{लंबा} \hi{है।} \hi{वह} \hi{मोटा} \hi{है।} \hi{वह} \hi{नाटा} \hi{है।}
\end{quote}

Five sentences, two people, and the only thing telling you which is which is the last letter of the adjective.
\end{tcolorbox}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}\hi{वह} \hi{लंबा} \hi{है}\textquotedblright{} and then \textquotedblleft{}\hi{वह} \hi{लंबी} \hi{है}\textquotedblright{}, hearing only the ending move
  \item the same pair with \textbf{\hi{पतला}}
  \item the same pair with \textbf{\hi{मोटा}}
  \item the same pair with \textbf{\hi{नाटा}}
  \item two sentences describing someone you know
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
In \textbf{\hi{वह} \hi{लंबी} \hi{है}}, which word tells you the person is a woman? (The adjective — \textbf{\hi{वह}} is the same for both.) What would the masculine sentence be? (\textbf{\hi{वह} \hi{लंबा} \hi{है}}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
